title: Articles & Prepositions
subtitle: The Tiny Spirits Who Run Everything
intro: They're small, but they're everywhere. The tiny spirits a, an, the, in, on and at appear in almost every sentence. Master them and your English instantly sounds more natural.

rules.title: A vs. An
rules.tagline: It's about the sound, not the letter

story.line: I found a apple and an unicorn!
An apple and a unicorn. Hehe. Say them out loud.
Use an before a vowel SOUND, and a before a consonant SOUND. Apple starts with an 'a' sound, so an apple.
But unicorn starts with u!
Listen: 'yoo-nicorn.' It starts with a 'y' sound, a consonant sound. So: a unicorn. And hour starts with a silent h, so: an hour.

parts.name: a + consonant sound
parts.detail: Including 'yoo' and 'w' sounds.
parts.example: a cat, a university, a one-time offer

parts.name: an + vowel sound
parts.detail: Including silent h.
parts.example: an egg, an hour, an honest man

parts.name: Letters and acronyms
parts.detail: Follow how the letter is said.
parts.example: an MRI (em-ar-eye), a UFO (yoo-ef-oh), an FBI agent

parts.name: Only for one countable thing
parts.detail: Not with plurals or uncountable nouns.
parts.example: a book (not a books, not a water)

rules.history:
A and an both come from the Old English word ān, which meant 'one.' Over time, the n dropped off before consonant sounds because 'an cat' was awkward to say, while 'an apple' kept it to stop two vowels from bumping together.

This split also explains some strange words: 'a napron' was misheard as 'an apron,' and 'a nadder' became 'an adder' (a type of snake)!
rules.trick: Trust your ears, not your eyes. Say the next word; if it starts with a vowel sound, add an n.

quiz.why: Umbrella starts with an 'uh' vowel sound.

rules.title: The (Definite Article)
rules.tagline: The specific one we both know about

story.line: I saw a cat in the garden. The cat was wearing a hat!
Notice what you did. First a cat, any cat, new to the listener. Then the cat, because now we both know which one.
So I say 'the sun,' because there's only one?
Yes. Use the when the listener knows which one: it's been mentioned, it's unique, or it's obvious from the situation.
Pass me the salt. Not a salt. The one right there! Hehe.

parts.name: Second mention
parts.detail: First a, then the.
parts.example: I bought a book. The book is great.

parts.name: Unique things
parts.detail: Only one exists.
parts.example: the sun, the moon, the internet

parts.name: Obvious from context
parts.detail: Both people know which one.
parts.example: Close the door, please.

parts.name: Superlatives & ordinals
parts.detail: the best, the first, the last.
parts.example: the tallest tower

parts.name: Some place names
parts.detail: Rivers, oceans, mountain ranges, plural countries.
parts.example: the Nile, the Pacific, the Alps, the United States

rules.history:
Old English had a whole family of words for 'the' that changed with gender and case: se, sēo, þæt and more. During the Middle English period, these collapsed into one simple form, þe, which became 'the.'

The old word þæt survives too: it became 'that.' And the 'ye' in 'Ye Olde Shoppe' is really 'the,' because the old letter þ (thorn) looked like a y in some printing.

examples.good: We swam in the Pacific Ocean.

rules.trick: A = 'one of many, you don't know which yet.' The = 'that one, you know the one.'

quiz.q: 'I have a dog. ___ dog is named Mochi.'

rules.title: No Article at All
rules.tagline: When to say nothing before a noun

story.line: I love the ramen! The life is the beautiful!
Too many 'the's! It sounds like a strange translation.
When you speak about things in general, use no article. 'I love ramen.' 'Life is beautiful.'
But I can say 'the ramen at this shop is amazing'?
Yes! That's a specific ramen. General = no article. Specific = the.

parts.name: General plurals
parts.detail: Talking about all of them.
parts.example: Cats are curious.

parts.name: General uncountables
parts.detail: Ideas, substances.
parts.example: Water is important. Love is strange.

parts.name: Names
parts.detail: Most people, cities, countries, languages.
parts.example: Hana lives in Kyoto and speaks Japanese.

parts.name: Meals, sports, school subjects
parts.detail: Usually no article.
parts.example: We had lunch. I play tennis. I study math.

parts.name: Fixed phrases
parts.detail: go to bed, go to school, at home, by train.
parts.example: She goes to school by bus.

rules.history:
Old English often used no article at all, and early English used 'the' far less than it does today. Over centuries, 'the' spread into many places where it had not been used before.

The general-versus-specific split is surprisingly hard for speakers of languages like Japanese, Korean, Chinese or Russian, which don't have articles at all, and for speakers of Spanish or French, which use the article for general statements ('La vida es bella').

examples.good: I go to school by bus.
examples.bad: I go to the school by the bus.

rules.trick: If you could add 'in general' to the end, drop the article: 'Music is fun (in general).'

rules.title: Much, Many, Few & Little
rules.tagline: Counting words for countable and uncountable nouns

story.line: How much onigiri do you have? I have much friends!
How many onigiri. And many friends!
Countable nouns use many and few. Uncountable nouns use much and little.
So I have little patience and few friends? Rude!
Careful, Yumi. 'A few' and 'a little' mean 'some, enough.' 'Few' and 'little' alone mean 'almost none.' The a changes the mood!

parts.name: Countable
parts.detail: many, few, a few, a number of, several.
parts.example: many books, a few friends

parts.name: Uncountable
parts.detail: much, little, a little, a great deal of.
parts.example: much time, a little sugar

parts.name: Both
parts.detail: some, any, a lot of, lots of, plenty of, no.
parts.example: a lot of books, a lot of water

parts.name: Few vs. a few
parts.detail: Few = not enough (negative). A few = some (positive).
parts.example: Few people came (sad). A few people came (okay!).

rules.history:
Many comes from Old English manig, and much from mycel (which meant 'big'). Mycel also gave Scots the word 'mickle.'

In modern speech, much sounds stiff in positive sentences. People say 'a lot of time' instead of 'much time,' but much is still natural in questions and negatives: 'Do you have much time?'
rules.trick: Many = more than you can count on your fingers. Much = more than fits in your bowl.

quiz.q: 'There are too ___ cars on the road.'

rules.title: In, On, At (Time)
rules.tagline: The triangle of time: from big to small

story.line: Hana, imagine an upside-down triangle. At the top, the wide part, is IN.
Big time periods: in 2026, in October, in summer, in the morning!
In the middle is ON: specific days and dates. On Monday, on my birthday, on October 24th.
And the sharp tip is AT! At 7 o'clock, at noon, at midnight!
Bigger box, IN. Day, ON. Exact point, AT.

parts.name: IN (big periods)
parts.detail: Years, months, seasons, centuries, parts of the day.
parts.example: in 1999, in June, in winter, in the evening

parts.name: ON (days and dates)
parts.detail: Days of the week, dates, special days.
parts.example: on Friday, on July 4th, on New Year's Day

parts.name: AT (exact times)
parts.detail: Clock times, and some fixed phrases.
parts.example: at 6:30, at noon, at night, at the weekend (UK)

parts.name: No preposition
parts.detail: Before this, next, last, every.
parts.example: I'll see you next Friday. (not on next Friday)

rules.history:
In, on and at all come from Old English (in, on, æt) and were originally about physical space. Over time English borrowed space words to talk about time. Linguists call this a metaphor: we imagine time as a place we move through.

That's why the time rules mirror the place rules: a big container (in), a surface (on), and an exact point (at).
rules.trick: The time triangle: IN (big) → ON (day) → AT (point).

quiz.why: On a day, at a time.

rules.title: In, On, At (Place)
rules.tagline: Inside, on a surface, or at a point

story.line: Where's Kaito? He's in the dojo, on the roof, at the door?
Those all mean different places!

IN = inside something with edges: in the box, in Tokyo. ON = on a surface or line: on the table, on the wall, on the train. AT = a point or a location for an activity: at the door, at school, at the bus stop.
I'm on the roof! Help! I'm stuck!
Hehe, I'll be at the ramen shop if anyone needs me.

parts.name: IN: enclosed spaces
parts.detail: Rooms, buildings, cities, countries, water.
parts.example: in the kitchen, in Japan, in the sea

parts.name: ON: surfaces and lines
parts.detail: Tables, walls, floors, streets, public transport.
parts.example: on the desk, on Main Street, on the bus

parts.name: AT: points and activities
parts.detail: Specific spots, addresses, events.
parts.example: at the corner, at 10 Main Street, at a concert

parts.name: Cars vs. buses
parts.detail: Small vehicles: in. Big ones you can walk in: on.
parts.example: in a car, in a taxi / on a bus, on a plane

rules.history:
These three prepositions have described space since Old English times. Ideas like 'on the bus' (but 'in the car') developed much later, once people rode public transport.

One theory: you can stand up and walk around on a bus, train or plane, like on a floor or platform, but you just sit inside a car.

examples.good: The picture is on the wall.
examples.bad: The picture is in the wall.

examples.good: I'll wait for you at the station.

rules.trick: IN = a box around you. ON = a floor under you. AT = a pin on the map.

rules.title: Ending a Sentence with a Preposition
rules.tagline: A myth that grammar spirits love to argue about

story.line: A strict ghost appears in the library, waving a ruler.
Who are you talking to?
The ghost insists you must say 'To whom are you talking?' because 'to' cannot end a sentence.
But 'Who are you talking to?' sounds totally normal!
Because it is normal. This 'rule' was invented by a poet who loved Latin. English has ended sentences with prepositions for over a thousand years.
Ghost-san, that's something you'll just have to put up with. Hehe.

parts.name: Totally fine
parts.detail: Questions, relative clauses, passives and phrasal verbs often end in a preposition.
parts.example: What are you looking at? This is the house I grew up in.

parts.name: Formal option
parts.detail: In very formal writing you may move the preposition earlier.
parts.example: This is the house in which I grew up.

parts.name: Avoid extra prepositions
parts.detail: Don't add a preposition that isn't needed.
parts.example: Where are you? (not Where are you at?) in formal writing

rules.history:
In 1672, the poet John Dryden criticized Ben Jonson for ending a line with a preposition. Dryden admired Latin, where a preposition can't end a sentence, so he wanted English to follow suit.

Schoolteachers repeated his opinion for centuries. But great writers including Shakespeare and Jane Austen ignored it. A well-known joke, often (and probably wrongly) credited to Winston Churchill, mocks the rule: 'This is the sort of nonsense up with which I will not put!'

examples.good: That's the friend I told you about.

rules.trick: If moving the preposition makes you sound like a Victorian ghost, leave it at the end.

quiz.q: Is 'Who did you go with?' correct English?
options: No, it must be 'With whom did you go?'
quiz.why: Ending with a preposition is standard English.

quiz.q: Who popularized the 'no preposition at the end' idea?
